deep.reconstruction:
Setting: §§502-508 (previous page) fix an odd prime q = 2p+1. Its quadratic residues are 1, α, β, γ, … (p of them) and its non-residues are 𝔞, 𝔟, …. The residues mod 2q, taken from squares coprime to 2q, are 1, A, B, C, … (also p of them, §505), and the non-residues mod 2q are 𝔄, 𝔅, …. This page relates the two lists, then begins the modulus 4q.

(top line, end of §508) Every residue A mod 2q, either as it stands or reduced by q, is a residue mod q.

§509. If A ≡ a² (mod 2q) with a odd, then q | a² − A. So A is a QR mod q, or A − q is when A > q. In modern terms: reduction mod q maps the squares mod 2q into the squares mod q.

§510. Odd QRs mod q are residues mod 2q (even residues mod 2q do not occur, since a is odd). Let α be odd and a² − α = nq.
- If a is odd, then a² − α is even. Since q is odd, n is even, so 2q | a² − α.

§511.
- If a is even, replace a by q − a, which is odd. Then (q − a)² − α = n'q with n' even, and again 2q divides it.
- Hence every odd QR α mod q lies in {1, A, B, …}.

§512. If α is even, then α + q is odd and is still a QR mod q. By §510-511 it is a residue mod 2q.

§513. Rule: the residues mod 2q are obtained from those mod q by keeping the odd ones and adding q to the even ones.
- Example: q = 7, residues {1, 2, 4} give {1, 9, 11}.
- (My gloss) This is just the CRT bijection between units mod 2q and units mod q: an odd representative r of a class mod q is either r or r + q.

§514. The same rule converts the non-residues.
- Example: q = 7, non-residues {3, 5, 6} give {3, 5, 13}.

§515. Divisor d = 4q.
- The number of units below d is φ(4)·φ(q) = 2·2p = 4p. Euler writes this as 2·1·2p.
- Besides a and d − a, two more roots give the same residue. Setting b − a = 2n and b + a = 2q gives b² − a² = 4nq, so b = 2q − a.
- So the four roots with equal square are a, 2q − a, 2q + a, 4q − a.

§516. There cannot be more than four such roots. This is asserted without proof (my justification: x² ≡ c mod 4 has 2 unit solutions and mod q has 2, so CRT gives 4). Hence:
- the number of residues is 4p/4 = p, the same as for q;
- the number of non-residues is 3p.

Tables:
- mod 12: residue 1; non-residues 5, 7, 11.
- mod 20: residues 1, 9; non-residues arranged as 3, 7 | 11, 19 | 13, 17.
- mod 28: residues 1, 9, 25; non-residues 3, 27, 19 | 5, 17, 13 | 11, 15, 23.

The arrangement (my observation) is exactly into cosets of the subgroup of squares. For example 3·{1, 9, 25} ≡ {3, 27, 19} (mod 28), 5·{1, 9, 25} ≡ {5, 17, 13} and 11·{1, 9, 25} ≡ {11, 15, 23}. The residues are listed as successive powers 1, 9, 9² ≡ 25. So implicitly the unit group mod 4q modulo squares is shown to have order 4, with the non-residues falling into three cosets.
errors: No mathematical errors found on this page.
§516: the claim that no more than four roots share a residue is asserted, not proved (Euler does not show that b − a and b + a must split the factor 4q exactly as chosen). The claim is true.
§515: the count 'φ(4q) = 2.1.2p' is written oddly (presumably φ(4)·φ(q) = 2·2p), but the value 4p is correct.
§509: the clause 'vel A − (2p+1), si fuerit A > 2p+1' is loosely phrased. The intended meaning is that A is reduced mod q, which is correct.

results.what: Quadratic residues mod 2q (q odd prime, units only) are obtained from those mod q: odd ones kept, even ones increased by q; same rule for non-residues; there are exactly p of each
results.modern_name: Chinese remainder theorem applied to quadratic residues; (Z/2q)* ≅ (Z/q)*
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Euler's own residue papers; systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 100-105

results.what: For modulus 4q, every unit square has exactly four roots a, 2q−a, 2q+a, 4q−a; hence p residues and 3p non-residues
results.modern_name: Number of square roots modulo composite moduli via CRT; index of the subgroup of squares in (Z/4q)* is 4
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801), arts. 103-105 (general count); Euler had such results in his residue papers

results.what: Tables of non-residues mod 20 and 28 arranged in cosets of the subgroup of squares
results.modern_name: Coset decomposition of (Z/n)* modulo its squares (Klein four-group quotient)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (residue/divisor classes of quadratic forms), Gauss (genus theory)

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary, well-known material from Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792, published 1849). The coset arrangement of the non-residue tables is a nice implicit group-theoretic touch, but it is consistent with Euler's known treatment of residue classes.

checkable.sympy: set(pow(x,2,28) for x in range(1,28) if gcd(x,28)==1) == {1,9,25}
set(pow(x,2,20) for x in range(1,20) if gcd(x,20)==1) == {1,9}
set(pow(x,2,12) for x in range(1,12) if gcd(x,12)==1) == {1}
checkable.asserts: Only unit residue mod 12 is 1; non-residues 5, 7, 11

checkable.sympy: all(set(pow(x,2,2*q) for x in range(1,2*q) if gcd(x,2*q)==1) == set(r if r%2 else r+q for r in set(pow(x,2,q) for x in range(1,q))) for q in primerange(3,200))
checkable.asserts: Rule §513: residues mod 2q = odd QRs mod q, plus even QRs increased by q

checkable.sympy: all(len(set(pow(x,2,4*q) for x in range(1,4*q) if gcd(x,4*q)==1)) == (q-1)//2 for q in primerange(3,200))
checkable.asserts: §516: number of unit residues mod 4q equals p = (q-1)/2

checkable.sympy: all(len([x for x in range(1,4*q) if gcd(x,4*q)==1 and pow(x,2,4*q)==pow(a,2,4*q)])==4 for q in primerange(3,60) for a in range(1,4*q) if gcd(a,4*q)==1)
checkable.asserts: §515-516: each unit square mod 4q has exactly four roots

checkable.sympy: all(pow(r,2,4*q)==pow(a,2,4*q) for q in primerange(3,60) for a in range(1,2*q,2) if a%q for r in [a, 2*q-a, 2*q+a, 4*q-a])
checkable.asserts: The four roots a, 2q−a, 2q+a, 4q−a share the same square mod 4q
The non-residue rows in the mod-28 table are cosets of the subgroup of squares
